title: How Does a Designer Develop Recognizable Codes?
author: RN Collins
principle: Evidence leads; atmosphere never substitutes for provenance.

narrativeSequence.caption: A designer develops recognizable codes by making recurring decisions legible across difference—not by repeating a logo, freezing one silhouette, or declaring an abstract aesthetic owned.
The record separates the material dress, House of Worth attribution, Charles Frederick Worth design credit, accession, and the museum’s present custody.

01 · NOTICE — What actually recurs?. Sample complete bodies of work, not isolated hero images. Code observable decisions—proportion, line, volume, material, construction, color, finish, movement, casting, image, language, refusal—and keep fact separate from critical interpretation.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 02 · NAME — Can the decision be described without mystique?. Write each code as a decision with range and rationale: what changes, what stays, what problem it solves, who contributes, and which exception proves that the principle is alive rather than decorative repetition.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 03 · TEST — Can another person recognize and challenge it?. Use blind comparisons, counterexamples, fittings, material trials, and collaborator critique. Record disagreement. If recognition depends entirely on founder explanation, the code has not yet become shared institutional knowledge.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

narrativeSequence.caption: 04 · BOUND — What is cultural signal, and what is a legal asset?. Separate reputation and visual resemblance from exact copyrighted expression, registered marks, design rights, contracts, confidential information, and other evidence. A codebook supports practice; it does not create a monopoly over style.
narrativeSequence.rights: Original publication graphic; no third-party imagery

mapping.prompt: Select twenty works across at least three moments and code only what can be observed.
Write five proposed codes, then attach two counterexamples and one deliberate exception to each.
Ask two collaborators to revise the descriptions and identify missing labor or influence.
Separate every cultural-recognition claim from the exact record supporting any legal right.
